overview: The Viceroyalty of Peru was a Spanish colonial government centered on Lima, made its capital in 1542. Its cities, mines and Indigenous communities were connected through commerce, craft and coercive labor. This card explains the wider history around the map’s 1650 to 1715 interval, including Indigenous criticism of colonial rule and the government’s eventual defeat.

periods.title: A colonial capital and voices of protest
periods.summary: Lima became a viceregal capital with institutions including San Marcos university. Guaman Poma’s illustrated chronicle later criticized exploitation and proposed reforms.

periods.title: The map’s selected interval
periods.summary: Mining and craftsmanship connected highland communities with colonial cities. Surviving cups and silverwork reveal Indigenous makers working within a society governed by Spain.

periods.title: Later institutions and independence
periods.summary: Lima’s hospital records reveal changing approaches to care and medical teaching. After independence was proclaimed in Lima in 1821, royal government continued in the highlands until the decisive defeat at Ayacucho in 1824.

sections.title: Water, silver and the cost of wealth

items.text: Potosí’s silver industry used artificial lakes and aqueducts to supply water-powered mills. Crushing and processing ore, then making coins, required a chain of specialized places and workers. A mountain of silver was also an enormous water-management problem.

Indigenous workers compelled to serve through the mita helped sustain Potosí’s wealth. Their neighborhoods lay apart from Spanish residents across an artificial river. The surviving city plan records an unequal social order as well as impressive engineering.

Mercury from Huancavelica helped process silver. The colonial draft-labor system sent workers into dangerous mining conditions and disrupted the communities supplying them. The heritage nomination for Santa Bárbara describes both this industrial connection and its human cost.

Lima’s builders combined local and European skills, adapting materials and techniques to earthquakes. Churches, hospitals, schools and houses were practical structures as well as statements of power. Their survival reflects repeated rebuilding, not a city preserved untouched since its founding.

Andean kero cups were often made in pairs for the ceremonial sharing of chicha, a fermented corn drink. Exchanging a drink could express a relationship between people. The paired vessels give historians evidence about social practice as well as carving skill.

A Quechua kero from seventeenth- or eighteenth-century Peru shows women, flowers and large parrots. Its feline handles changed how the decorated surface could be arranged. Traces of colored resin remind us that a worn museum object could once have looked much brighter.

Some colonial Andean textiles incorporated Chinese animals and peonies inspired by imported silks. Materials and designs crossed oceans before local makers adapted them. A tapestry can therefore preserve evidence of connections far beyond the town where it was woven.

A gold cup recovered from the Atocha shipwreck of 1622 was designed to hold a bezoar, a stone-like deposit from a camelid’s stomach. People believed it could counter poison. That belief explains the object; it does not establish that the treatment worked. An expensive cup could carry a very questionable health accessory.

A highland lectern from around 1700 combined a wooden core with worked silver sheets showing angels and elaborate foliage. Such objects required coordination between different crafts. Their gleaming surfaces can hide the less glamorous structure that made them usable.

San Marcos university was founded in Lima in 1551. Higher education became one of the colonial capital’s enduring institutions. A university’s existence, however, tells us about an institution; it does not mean that all children in the viceroyalty could attend school.

San Andrés hospital’s admission books from 1711 to 1714 recorded patients’ origins, marital status and family descent. October 1713 entries included a free child and adult classified using a colonial mixed-ancestry category. These were exceptions to the hospital’s usual identification with Spanish patients.

Later in the colonial period, theatre rent helped support San Andrés hospital. The theatre reopened in 1761 and was leased for income. Entertainment and care were linked through a very concrete financial arrangement: a performance venue could help pay hospital expenses.

An anatomical teaching space opened at San Andrés in 1792. Medical students learned there, connecting the hospital with professional education. This later development belongs to the viceroyalty’s history after the map’s selected interval.

In 1792, digging a deep bone-storage pit at the hospital reached groundwater. An official worried about nearby household wells, and advisers recommended partly filling the excavation with rubble, lime and brick. The record preserves a sanitation concern and proposed response, not proof that contamination or illness occurred.

sections.title: An Indigenous author and a writing sample

items.text: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala wrote and illustrated a long critique of Spanish colonial government. His manuscript combines Spanish with substantial Quechua passages and proposes reforms. It preserves a particular Indigenous author’s arguments, rather than a single view shared by every Andean community.

The title includes the Spanish words “buen gobierno”, meaning “good government”. This short sample follows the Royal Danish Library’s catalog transcription of his manuscript title, using ordinary Latin letters. The phrase captures his demand for a better way to govern; his criticism was itself part of colonial history.

ending.text: Independence was proclaimed in Lima in 1821, but the royal government continued in the southern highlands. Sucre’s victory at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 brought the decisive royal capitulation. The map’s 1715 endpoint precedes these events by more than a century; it is not the viceroyalty’s historical end.
